summary: Round 3, scoped to the delta since a2fe44ad. All five minors and both test-reviewer majors are genuinely fixed, and the two I was asked to verify hardest hold up: the delta-counter reset in a `finally` is correct on every path that reaches the store (success clears `dirty`, IOException and unchecked throw both reset the counter and leave `dirty` set, the `!dirty || closed` early return correctly resets nothing, and `written` is assigned only after `putIfAbsent` returns so the flag cannot be cleared without reaching the store nor left set after a landed write that the same key's retry will resolve); and F14's reorder closes the window rather than moving it -- a throw inside the offsets loop now leaves both `pendingStreams` and `pendingSequence` at their old values, and the one remaining skew (streams ahead of sequence) is harmless because ChainReplay.fold merges absolute lastOffset+1 with Math::max, which I checked at ChainReplay.java:391-399 rather than taking from the comment. The cost lens is clean: checkpoint PUTs are per chain at most max(commits/K, 1/T), `slot` is hardcoded 0 in LogKeys.logPrefix, the dirty flag holds an idle chain at zero requests (R3), no LIST or GET is added, and nothing here scales with records, shards, partitions or indices. Six minors, none blocking under review.md rule minors-land. The one I would actually fix is F17: the backlog-done row states the `putIfAbsent`-fences-a-stale-leader rationale that F13 retracted, in its own bullet, and refutes it 3,000 characters later -- the row catalogues that error class without correcting it at the site. F18 is the one with real teeth: the ticker's InterruptedException branch reads ANY interrupt as shutdown and logs nothing, so a store using the textbook restore-and-throw idiom -- which BoundedLock.takeOrFail:56 in this same package already uses -- silently and permanently kills the T trigger. PROCESS NOTE, not a finding: two distinct diff hashes already carry M4.8b2 verdicts, so this is round 3 against the cap of two, and there is no `rounds:M4.8b2` line in baselines/review.txt, which is neither modified nor staged. check-reviewed.sh will refuse the commit until one is added (review.md rule two-round-cap: keyed first field, a reason after it, rendered as an ADDED line in a staged baselines/review.txt).

findings.title: The retracted putIfAbsent rationale is left standing in its own bullet, and refuted later in the same row
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land: on a pass a minor is recorded in the commit body and the commit lands.
findings.failure_scenario: The row asserts: 'putIfAbsent, NOT put ... an unconditional put lets a leader that does not yet know it is fenced overwrite its successor's checkpoint.' That is the claim F13 retracted and the code comment at CheckpointWriter.java:201-205 now explicitly calls impossible -- the epoch is inside the key via LogKeys.logPrefix(), so leaders at E and E+1 never address one key. The same row says so 3,000 characters downstream, in the 'FOUR TIMES ... AN INVENTED REASON' bullet, which names this very instance. So the authoritative landed record both states and refutes it. Concretely: whoever picks up M4.8c (newest-checkpoint discovery) or M4.10 (idempotency) reads the row top-down, takes the first bullet as the property of the checkpoint key, and designs discovery or a takeover path on the belief that a conditional write fences a stale leader out of a successor's checkpoint. It does not; nothing does, because the two leaders write different keys. This is the error class M4.43's own row names -- 'a false claim corrected in one copy while its duplicate stood' -- and the row lists 'the NFR-2 argument left standing in a TEST javadoc after production retracted it' as an instance of it while committing the same error one bullet earlier. The NFR-2 case IS corrected at its own site in this row; the putIfAbsent one is not. Fix: strike the causal clause, leaving the M4 SPEC citation, and let the later bullet carry the retraction.

findings.title: The ticker reads ANY interrupt as shutdown, so the T trigger can die silently and permanently
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land. Recorded rather than blocking because the only interrupt source in today's tree is close(); it becomes reachable with the first store that restores the flag.
findings.failure_scenario: F12's restructure is right as far as it goes -- an unchecked throw from a Ticker or from writeOnTick now hits `catch (Throwable keepTicking)` and the thread survives -- but the InterruptedException branch beside it restores the flag and returns UNCONDITIONALLY, never consulting `closed`, and logs nothing, while its sibling two lines below logs precisely because 'WITHOUT THIS THE T TRIGGER DIES SILENTLY AND PERMANENTLY'. BatchingSequencer.drainLoop faced the identical question and answers it: `return running ? stopping : null`, on the stated reasoning that a delegate using the textbook idiom (`Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new IOException`) leaves the flag set on a thread nobody asked to stop. That idiom is already in this package at BoundedLock.takeOrFail:56 and is what any HTTP/S3 backend will do for ClosedByInterruptException. Concrete path, live only because F12 pulled the write inside this try: store.putIfAbsent restores the flag and throws IOException; writeIfDirty catches it at line 213, logs, returns normally; tickForever loops to ticker.awaitNextTick(), whose Thread.sleep throws InterruptedException immediately on the still-set flag; this branch returns with `closed == false` and NOTHING logged. On a cluster committing fewer than K deltas per period -- the case the class says the T trigger is all there is for -- no checkpoint is written again for the life of the process, and M4.9's bounded recovery silently degrades back to the unbounded full-chain replay it exists to replace, with no signal anywhere. Direct answer to the question asked: a write-path InterruptedException cannot be mistaken for shutdown WITHIN one iteration, because writeOnTick declares no checked InterruptedException -- it is mistaken for one on the NEXT iteration. The vice-versa direction also fires: a close() interrupt landing mid-PUT surfaces as an IOException inside writeIfDirty and logs 'checkpoint at sequence N was not written; retrying at the next trigger' (lines 221-223) during a shutdown that will never retry, sending an operator after a retry that cannot happen. Fix: `if (closed) return;` else log and keep ticking, exactly as drainLoop distinguishes.

findings.title: The finally is correct for every throw that reaches the store, but its comment claims a scope the try does not have
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land. The request-rate half the finally was added for is genuinely covered; what is wrong is the sentence.
findings.failure_scenario: `new Checkpoint(...)` (line 195) and `checkpoint.encode()` (line 196) sit OUTSIDE the try, while the comment says 'RESET ON EVERY EXIT, INCLUDING AN UNCHECKED THROW'. The Checkpoint canonical constructor validates and throws IllegalArgumentException on a blank podId, a negative lastAppliedFlushSeq, a negative nextOffset or oldestRetainedOffset past nextOffset; encode() allocates the whole body. If either throws, deltasSinceCheckpoint stays at or above K, so EVERY subsequent commit re-enters writeIfDirty, throws again, and is swallowed by observe's catch (Throwable) with a WARNING and a stack trace -- one per commit, at the full commit rate, forever, with no checkpoint ever written. No PUT is issued (the throw precedes the store call), so this is a log-volume and never-recovers defect rather than the request-rate defect the finally removed; the reachable triggers are narrow TODAY only because CommitRequest's own constructor already refuses blank podIds and negative flushSeqs, which is a guarantee two records away from the sentence relying on it. Moving the two statements inside the try makes the comment true and costs nothing.

findings.title: The new putIfAbsent comment has one reachable counter-example, and the Optional that would detect it is discarded
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land. The consequence is transient and in the safe direction for M4.10.
findings.failure_scenario: The rewritten rationale is much closer than the one it replaced, but it rests on 'neither pods nor pendingStreams can move without pendingSequence moving too', and `capture` advances `pods` FIRST, in its own loop at line 129, before the offsets loop F14 reordered. observe swallows Throwable, so a throw anywhere between line 129 and line 154 leaves the process alive with `pods` advanced and `pendingSequence` unmoved -- the same window F14 was written for, on the one field the reorder does not cover. Sequence: a PUT reports IOException and had landed; a later commit throws mid-capture after pods.merge; the next trigger re-encodes the SAME sequence with a larger pods map; BinStore.putIfAbsent returns Optional.empty(), which its own javadoc (BinStore.java:54-57) defines as ALREADY EXISTS and explicitly not an error; this code ignores the return value, sets written = true and clears dirty. The checkpoint at that sequence then permanently carries the older pod watermarks while the writer believes it wrote the newer ones, and nothing logs the divergence. Impact is bounded -- the watermarks are re-derived at the next sequence, and for M4.10 a watermark that is too LOW replays a duplicate rather than dropping a real flush -- which is why this is minor. It is recorded because 'cannot' is the load-bearing word in a comment about a conditional write, because the finally fix added a second route the comment does not name (an unchecked store throw that landed, not only an IOException that did), and because discarding Optional<Version> throws away the one signal that distinguishes 'I wrote it' from 'something else is already here'. Checked and NOT defects: pods running ahead of pendingSequence in a written checkpoint is safe, since pods only advances after log.commitAll returned, so the deltas it accounts for are in the chain and are replayed from seq; and pendingStreams ahead of pendingSequence -- the direction F14 deliberately chose -- is safe because ChainReplay.fold merges absolute lastOffset+1 with Math::max (ChainReplay.java:391-399), so re-applying a delta already folded in is idempotent.

findings.title: F16's replacement note justifies an allocation cost by comparing it to an I/O latency
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land. No request rate is affected; this is the prose the fix added, which is exactly the surface this round inherits.
findings.failure_scenario: The new note says the O(all streams) copy is 'bounded by the commit rate and dwarfed by the delta PUT beside it'. Those are different quantities. performance.md rule 3 makes allocation a first-class result -- 'a change 5% faster that allocates 2x more is a regression' -- and its gate table names allocation per record the leading indicator of GC-driven collapse; a PUT dwarfs this on the clock while allocating almost nothing, so the comparison cannot support the conclusion. What the commit path now does is build the whole stream table TWICE per commit: Map.copyOf inside offsets(), then a fresh LinkedHashMap of new StreamOffsets in capture (lines 146-152), on the single BatchingSequencer committer thread that every producer in the fleet queues behind, for a result consumed once per K. At the 1,600 streams Checkpoint's own javadoc uses and the 20 commits/s BatchingSequencer documents for its 50 ms interval, that is roughly 64,000 short-lived objects per second added to the one path the $52/month depends on, with 999 of every 1,000 copies discarded at the shipped K = 1000, no benchmark and no measurement -- and this note is what a future reader will cite as the reason not to look (performance.md rule 8 accepts a note in place of a benchmark, so the note has to be right). A capture-on-demand flag set by the ticker would make the copy once per checkpoint instead of once per commit. Adjacent and recorded rather than filed separately: writeOnTick is synchronized and holds the writer monitor across the PUT while observe needs the same monitor, so a slow checkpoint PUT stalls the committer thread for its duration -- the class comment 'A FAILED CHECKPOINT NEVER FAILS A COMMIT' invites the reader to think the commit path is insulated, and it is insulated from a failed one but not from a slow one. Same magnitude as the K trigger, which already PUTs inline on that thread, so it is an observation rather than a second defect.

findings.title: 'A node that lost or released its lease must not PUT into the chain's prefix at all' is stated as a guarantee and implemented as best-effort
findings.blocks_reason: review.md rule minors-land. The escaping PUT is truthful and epoch-scoped, so the consequence is benign; the comment is what overstates.
findings.failure_scenario: close() sets `closed` and interrupts but is not synchronized and does not join the ticker thread, and the `closed` test at line 191 is inside the monitor the ticker already holds while its PUT is in flight. So when the renewer fences the node (LocalSequencer.java:126-133, new in this diff) or LocalSequencer.close() runs (lines 378-381) while the ticker sits between line 191 and line 210, LocalSequencer proceeds straight to leases.release() and one checkpoint PUT lands under the old epoch's prefix after the term is gone. Here that is harmless -- the epoch is in the key, the object describes a chain state that was already committed, and M4.8b1's filter keeps ckpt/ keys out of chain replay -- which is why it is minor. It is worth recording because BatchingSequencer.close JOINS its committer before touching the delegate for the strictly analogous reason it spells out ('running it while the committer is still inside CommitLog's redrive loop lets a retry win a slot AFTER this node gave up its term'), so a reader comparing the two will take the guard comment here as the same strength of guarantee, and it is not one. Either join the ticker in close(), or say best-effort and say why it is enough.
